suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `end` is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` — an exact duplicate of `start` — instead of using `slotEndTime`. WHY: the working-hours upper-bound test `end > workingHour.endTime` therefore compares the slot START against the working-day end, so a slot whose start is inside working hours but whose end (start + eventLength) overruns `workingHour.endTime` is never filtered and is reported as available, allowing bookings outside the host's working hours. HOW: compute `const end = slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute();`.

suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: when `dateOverrideExist` is true the function returns `true` before running the `busy.every(...)` check at the end. HOW: do not return early here; fall through so the override branch only decides whether the slot is inside the override window, and let the existing `busy` evaluation decide availability (e.g. `if (dateOverrideExist) { /* within override, still check busy */ } else { /* fall through to busy */ }`).

suggestions.suggestionContent: The message shown for a rejected email disagrees with the reason the code is reacting to. This branch fires when the server rejected the email (result.errors.email), and this PR gives that condition its own server string — user.email.blocked, added in config/locales/server.en.yml as "is not allowed." — but the client re-labels it with the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid'). A user whose address is perfectly well-formed but blocked/hosted on a blacklisted domain is therefore told their email is invalid, contradicting the reason just returned by the server. Use the blocked/not-allowed message (and add a matching client locale key) instead of user.email.invalid. Notice the same generic string is used at line ~94 for validation failures, so it should not be reused to represent a distinct server-side rejection.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: This test is named "returns false if a record with the email doesn't exist," but it cannot verify that. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` returns `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`, which yields `nil` (not `false`) when no record exists, and under this suite's RSpec 2 semantics `subject.should be_false` is a truthiness matcher that passes for any falsy value including `nil`. The assertion therefore passes on the nil the code actually returns and would only fail on an outright `true`; it does not pin the `false`/`nil` distinction its name asserts. Assert the value exactly (e.g. `subject.should == false`, or `be_falsey`/`be_nil` if nil is intended) so a regression returning a non-false falsy value is caught.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `should_block?` is declared/used as a boolean predicate (its name, its use in the validator's boolean context, and `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:23`'s `be_false`), but the expression `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]` returns `nil` when no record matches instead of `false`. Coerce the result to a real boolean (e.g. `record.present? && record.action_type == actions[:block]`), otherwise the method's return contract as declared by its consumer/spec is violated.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: tu is not checked for nil before use. TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id]) returns nil whenever the logged-in user has no topic_users row for that topic (the same lookup TopicUser.get performs), and the next line dereferences tu.notification_level, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500. Because the route is only gated by ensure_logged_in, any logged-in user can hit /t/:topic_id/unsubscribe(.json) for a topic they never opened and trigger the crash. Guard the lookup, e.g. `tu = TopicUser.find_by(...); return render json: {success: false} unless tu` (or build/return early) before reading notification_level.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: The unsubscribe endpoint mutates notification_level (tu.save!) via a plain GET route (config/routes.rb:440-441) with skip_before_filter :check_xhr, authenticating only through the session cookie. There is no CSRF token (Rails forgery protection does not cover GET) and no capability token, unlike EmailController#unsubscribe which authorizes via DigestUnsubscribeKey. Any third-party page can embed and, when a logged-in user loads it, silently change that user's notification_level for the topic. Require a per-user capability token (like the digest unsubscribe key) in the URL, or perform the state change from an authenticated non-GET request that carries the CSRF token.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `TopicUser.find_by(...)` can return nil (e.g. the user clicks the emailed unsubscribe link for a topic for which no TopicUser row was ever created), and the very next line dereferences it (`tu.notification_level > ...`, then `tu.save!`). This raises NoMethodError on nil and the unsubscribe request 500s. Guard the nil case (e.g. return early or use `TopicUser.change`/`find_or_create_by`) before reading/writing notification_level.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The `unsubscribe_link` translation now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}` (config/locales/server.en.yml), but `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` is only given `unsubscribe_url` when the caller supplies it (user_notifications.rb:295). Any other email built with `add_unsubscribe_link: true` but no `unsubscribe_url` will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument inside html_part at send time. Pass a default unsubscribe_url into template_args (or guard the interpolation) so the new placeholder is always satisfiable.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The `unsubscribe_url` added to the `message_with_unsubscribe` fixture is never asserted. The two tests only check that the List-Unsubscribe header `be_present` and that the body matches `user_preferences_url`; neither references `unsubscribe_url`. So they would still pass if the topic-specific unsubscribe URL this PR introduces were dropped or wired to the wrong value. Add an assertion (e.g. that `message_with_unsubscribe.body` matches `/t/1234/unsubscribe`, and that the List-Unsubscribe header points at the topic unsubscribe URL) so the new behaviour is actually covered.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: The title is interpolated unescaped and then emitted with triple braces. The controller (topic-unsubscribe.js.es6:6) builds stopNotificiationsText via I18n.t with { title: model.fancyTitle }, which performs no escaping, and this template renders it as {{{stopNotificiationsText}}}. Combined with the locale string "...notifications for {{title}}." (config/locales/client.en.yml:985), any markup in the topic title is injected as raw HTML. Escape the title before interpolation (or render the composed value escaped) so user-authored titles cannot inject HTML.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (find_by yields nil when no row exists), but the next lines dereference it unconditionally (`tu.notification_level`, `tu.save!`). Since the new unsubscribe routes are public GET endpoints, any logged-in user visiting /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe for a topic they have never tracked will trigger a NoMethodError and a 500 instead of a sane response. Guard the nil case (e.g. create/skip or redirect) before reading notification_level.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: Unescaped output of user-controlled content in the response. {{{stopNotificiationsText}}} uses a triple stache (no HTML escaping), and the controller builds that string by interpolating the raw topic title (`title: this.get("model.fancyTitle")`, topic-unsubscribe.js.es6:6) into an i18n string containing markup. A topic whose title contains HTML/script is injected verbatim into the unsubscribe page (stored XSS). Escape the title before interpolation, or render with escaped braces and put the <strong> in the template.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: website_name re-exposes the user's website for profiles where it is intentionally hidden — the attribute is added to the public `attributes` list (line 43) but not to `untrusted_attributes`, and `include_website_name` only checks `website.present?` instead of `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`. WHY: `website` is an untrusted attribute gated by `restrict_user_fields?` (lib/guardian/user_guardian.rb:58-60), which is true for a TL0 user viewed by an anonymous visitor; `website_name` derives `website_host + path` from the same `object.user_profile.website`, so the URL that `include_website?` suppresses is still disclosed through the new key (the existing spec at spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb:11-14 only asserts the listed untrusted keys are absent, so this leak is not covered). HOW: add `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list (or have `include_website_name` return false when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`), mirroring the `website` handling.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `include_website_name` is missing the trailing `?` required by ActiveModelSerializers. WHY: every other conditional-inclusion guard in this file uses the `?` form (`define_method "include_#{attr}?"` at lines 9/18/27, `include_email?` at line 117), and AMS 0.8.3 resolves the guard as `include_<attr>?`; because this method lacks the `?` it is never invoked, so the intended `website.present?` condition is silently ignored and `website_name` is always serialized. HOW: rename to `def include_website_name?`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: the `elsif` branch treats the last two dot-segments as the registrable domain, so multi-part public suffixes are mis-compared. WHY: for e.g. website_host='example.co.uk' and discourse_host='forum.co.uk' both have 3 segments, the branch compares `'co.uk' == 'co.uk'`, concludes the domains match, and returns `website_host + path`, even though example.co.uk and forum.co.uk are unrelated sites — the display then shows a path that does not belong to the instance domain, defeating the feature's purpose. HOW: compare against a public-suffix-aware registrable domain (e.g. use the PublicSuffix list) or require at least the full suffix before treating hosts as the same domain, instead of blindly taking `split('.')[1..-1]`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The guard method is named `include_website_name`, but ActiveModelSerializers (and this file's own convention, e.g. `include_email?` at line 117) resolves per-attribute guards via `include_<attribute>?`. Because the name lacks the trailing `?`, the framework never invokes it: the `website.present?` guard is dead code and `website_name` is serialized unconditionally, emitting `website_name: null` for users without a website. Rename to `include_website_name?`.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new `website_name` compares two domain names case-sensitively. `URI(website.to_s).host` preserves the letter case written by the user, whereas `Discourse.current_hostname` is the canonical lower-cased host, and no side is down-cased before the comparison at lines 141, 144-146 and 149 (including the `ends_with?` suffix check). Because DNS host names are case-insensitive identity values, `http://EXAMPLE.com/user` and `http://example.com/user` denote the same host but take different branches, so the same-site check is decided by letter case: the wrong arm is chosen and the full-path form is dropped. Normalise both sides before comparing, e.g. `website_host = URI(website.to_s).host&.downcase` (or use `URI(...).hostname`, which down-cases) and compare against `Discourse.current_hostname.to_s.downcase`.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: `website_name` is derived from the same `object.user_profile.website` value that `:website` protects via `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), but it is only gated by `include_website_name` -> `website.present?`. Since the untrusted filter removes `website` for some viewers while `website_name` is still emitted, and in the same-domain / subdomain branches it returns host *plus* `URI(website).path` (lines 143/146/149), the user's full website URL still leaves in the response for viewers the filter was supposed to strip it from. Either add `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes` or gate `include_website_name` with the same trust condition as `website`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The conditional-inclusion guard is named `include_website_name`, but ActiveModelSerializers resolves these guards as `include_<attribute>?` (the sibling in this very file is `include_email?` at line 117). As written the method is never called, so the guard is dead and the `:website_name` attribute declared at line 43 is serialized unconditionally. That defeats the intent of the guard (`website.present?`): the payload now always carries `website_name`, including for the scopes where `website` itself is withheld by the `untrusted_attributes` list (line 109), leaking the user's site host/path to viewers who were never meant to receive the website. Rename the method to `include_website_name?` so the serializer base class honors it.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new `website_name` field is gated only on `website.present?`, ignoring the visibility constraint this file declares for its source attribute: lines 105-111 put `:website` in `untrusted_attributes`, so `website` is omitted for viewers not allowed to see profile fields, but `website_name` is still serialized because `include_website_name` never consults that condition. Those viewers now receive the user's URL host, and when the host equals (lines 141-143) or is a parent of (144-149) the instance host they receive host + path, i.e. the complete URL that `website` was supposed to hide. Fix by adding `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list (105-111) — or make the guard reuse `website`'s own inclusion condition instead of a bare presence check.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: runShardSplitQuery now interpolates every target via datasource.applyTemplateVariables (line 52), but it then delegates each sub-request to runSplitQuery (line 163), which this PR also changed to call datasource.applyTemplateVariables again (querySplitting.ts:299), so each target is interpolated (and ad hoc filters applied) twice. WHY: double interpolation re-runs addAdHocFilters on an already-filtered expression; the stream-selector path masks the duplicate via labelExists() dedup in addFilterToStreamSelector (modifyQuery.ts:494), but parsed/structured-metadata labels use addFilterAsLabelFilter which does not dedup, producing duplicated label filters, and any interpolated value containing '$' can be re-interpolated. This is confirmed by the updated test expecting applyTemplateVariables toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5) for a single target (1 call here + 4 sub-requests through runSplitQuery) instead of 1. HOW: interpolate only once — either remove the interpolation added to runShardSplitQuery and let runSplitQuery do it, or have splitQueriesByStreamShard pass the already-interpolated targets without re-interpolating in runSplitQuery.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: Interpolating (line 299) before the splitting partition (line 300) breaks the `$__range` guard. `querySupportsSplitting`/`isQueryWithRangeVariable` deliberately keeps queries with `$__range` out of splitting because that variable is interpolated against the split time range and would be wrong (see the comment at lines 285-287). applyTemplateVariables/templateSrv.replace substitutes built-in variables like `$__range`/`$__interval`/`$__auto`, so by the time `partition(... !querySupportsSplitting(query))` runs the expression no longer contains `$__range`, the guard returns false, and such queries are now split — producing range-windowed results computed against each chunk instead of the whole query range. Keep the range-variable check on the un-interpolated expression: run the partition/querySupportsSplitting test on the raw targets (or capture the raw expr before mapping) and only interpolate the queries that actually go to execution.

suggestions.label: no_defect
suggestions.suggestionContent: The `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters))` is correctly covered by the new test. If removed, the expr reaching runQuery would retain `$__auto` and step would remain `$step`.

suggestions.label: no_defect

suggestions.suggestionContent: detectProvider() no longer fails fast when multiple CryptoProviders are present and instead silently picks the first after sorting by order() descending. All Keycloak providers return the same order (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200), so a tie between two providers is broken by the non-deterministic ServiceLoader iteration order rather than the intended priority. The previous code threw an IllegalStateException forcing the classpath to be corrected; now a deployment with two provider jars (exactly the 'multiple providers on classpath' scenario this PR enables) can silently select the unintended provider — e.g. a non-FIPS/strict provider when FIPS is required — with no error. In a FIPS deployment containing both crypto-default and crypto-fips1402, a non-FIPS provider can be selected silently, defeating FIPS. Give FIPS a strictly higher order (e.g. 400) so it always wins, or keep fail-fast on ambiguous equal-order providers.

Because the decoder it reads back with (ASN1Decoder.readLength) accepts non-canonical long-form lengths (e.g. 0x81) and validates only tag numbers, a regression in ASN1Encoder.writeLength that always emitted long form would still round-trip and the test would still pass, even though the produced signature would no longer be valid DER and would be rejected by the Keycloak server / a JDK Signature.verify. Assert the encoded signature is valid DER (e.g. verify it with a JDK Signature, or compare asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign) against a known-good width-padded r||s and assert its length equals algorithm.getSignatureLength()).

WHY: The local path stores only hashed codes (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes into secretData), but this user-storage path hands the plaintext one-time codes to the provider, so they are persisted in cleartext in external storage (the test provider stores input.getChallengeResponse() verbatim), exposing reusable credentials to anyone with read access to that store. HOW: Pass the already-hashed representation (the credentialModel built from createFromValues) rather than the raw code list, as the local provider does.

suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: getCredentials builds the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel via createFromValues but never sets its id from the stored myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() (createFromValues does not populate id). WHY: The returned federated model has a null id, so callers that identify/delete the credential by id — e.g. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) when all codes are used, or federated-credential deletion via getFederatedCredentialsStream — cannot target the actual credential. HOW: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after createFromValues.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: Recovery-code verification compares the submitted credential against each stored code with `key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())`, a short-circuiting, non-constant-time String comparison. Combined with anyMatch (which stops at the first match), success/failure timing depends on the number of matching leading characters and on match index, leaking information about the secret recovery codes. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. MessageDigest.isEqual on the byte arrays, or the same constant-time helper used elsewhere for credential verification) for each candidate instead of String.equals.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes `generatedCodes` (the raw, unhashed recovery codes from the form) with JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString and passes them as the UserCredentialModel value, which user-storage providers persist verbatim as the credential's credentialData (see BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential -> setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())). The DB path instead stores the hashed codes via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues. This leaves the recovery codes in cleartext in user storage, an invalid credential state that breaks the invariant that recovery codes are stored hashed. Serialize/hash the codes (e.g. derive the same value the credential provider stores, or hash each code) instead of writing the raw generated codes.

suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator reimplements get_item_key/value_from_cursor exactly like the numeric Paginator (math.floor/ceil on a raw attribute) instead of DateTimePaginator, yet the only caller (organization_auditlogs.py:76-83) uses it with order_by='-datetime'. WHY: item.datetime is a DateTimeField (models/auditlogentry.py:69), so math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError inside build_cursor on the first non-empty page, returning a 500 for the exact endpoint this class was added for; value_from_cursor also returns the raw cursor value rather than converting to a datetime, so the build_queryset comparison against the datetime column would be wrong even if the floor/ceil call were fixed. HOW: subclass DateTimePaginator (or copy its get_item_key/value_from_cursor datetime conversion) in OptimizedCursorPaginator so the key extraction matches the -datetime ordering used by the endpoint.

suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The advanced branch slices the queryset with a negative start offset (queryset[cursor.offset:stop] when cursor.offset < 0). WHY: cursor.offset is parsed verbatim from the user-supplied cursor query parameter (Cursor.from_string, cursors.py:52-61, no sign check) and Django does not support negative indexing on QuerySet slices — it produces an invalid negative OFFSET / raises, so sending a cursor with a negative offset when optimized_pagination is enabled yields a 500; the comment claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is incorrect. HOW: reject negative offsets (raise BadPaginationError/ParseError) instead of slicing with them, or clamp start_offset to 0 before slicing.

suggestions.suggestionContent: The added comment says this change will "allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination ... safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions", but the statement it annotates, line 182, is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` — it clamps negative offsets to 0, i.e. it does the opposite of what the comment claims and leaves the 'negative offset' (offset < 0) paging behaviour exactly as before. The comment is now untrue for the code it sits on; either drop the 'allow negative offsets' wording or make the code actually permit them.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment here claims "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" and that passing a negative `start_offset` is "safe", but Django QuerySet slicing rejects negative indices (`AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so `list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with a negative start_offset cannot work. The prose documents ORM behaviour that does not exist and calls the path safe; either correct the comment or remove the unsupported negative-offset branch. (The class docstring at lines 826-828 advertises this same 'Negative offset support'.)

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The advanced-pagination branch slices the queryset with a negative start offset (`start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0`). Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise "Negative indexing is not supported", so any request that reaches this branch throws an unhandled exception. The branch is reachable: the audit-log endpoint enables `enable_advanced_features` for superusers/global-access members, and `cursor.offset` is attacker-controlled via `Cursor.from_string` (`?optimized_pagination=true&cursor=0:-1:0` => offset -1). Clamp to a valid non-negative range or reject negative offsets instead of slicing with them; the comment claiming the ORM handles negative slicing is incorrect.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` subclasses `BasePaginator` but its `get_item_key` (and the `self.desc` used at line 903) rely on attributes `self.key` and `self._is_asc` that are set up by the concrete `DateTimePaginator`, not by `BasePaginator`. This method was copied verbatim from the datetime paginator, which suggests the class was meant to extend a cursor/datetime paginator. As written, instantiating it and calling `get_item_key` raises AttributeError (missing `self.key`/`self._is_asc`) before any results are produced. Subclass the appropriate concrete paginator (or initialize `key`/`desc`/`_is_asc`) so the attributes exist.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The branch declares it enables negative-offset pagination and comments that `The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically`, but it does not: Django QuerySet slicing rejects a negative `start` (it asserts "Negative indexing is not supported"), and `start_offset = cursor.offset` explicitly passes the negative value straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. So this code cannot behave as described — if a cursor ever carries a negative offset it raises instead of returning a page. Nothing in the cursor construction path (`build_cursor`, `Cursor.offset`) generates a negative offset, so the branch is also effectively dead for the feature it claims to implement. Either remove the branch/false claim, or convert the negative offset into a positive slice bound before slicing.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment declares this change `allow[s] negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination`, but the actual computation is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which clamps non-prev offsets at 0 — i.e. it never permits a negative offset. The declared optimization is a no-op relative to the original `queryset[offset:stop]`; the comment describes behavior the code does not have.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The negative-offset branch slices with a negative start plus a positive stop: `start_offset = cursor.offset` (e.g. -5), `stop = start_offset + limit + extra` (e.g. 95), then `queryset[-5:95]`. A negative slice start is relative to the END of the data, so for a dataset larger than `stop` the resolved start (`N-5`) exceeds `stop` and the slice returns an EMPTY list; for other offsets it returns rows from the tail rather than the requested page. The comment's claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is wrong — for an unsliced queryset Django materializes the whole queryset and applies Python slice semantics (and raises IndexError for negative slicing on a sliced queryset). The advertised 'advanced' pagination therefore yields empty/wrong pages instead of the requested range. Clamp the start (e.g. use `max(0, ...)`, or map negative offsets to positive ones based on a known total) and slice a non-negative range.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies integer math directly to the raw field value: `int(math.floor(value) ... math.ceil(value))`. The endpoint that consumes this paginator (organization_auditlogs.py line 79) passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a datetime and `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError. The pre-existing DateTimePaginator path this replaces is datetime-aware, so the new paginator's key contract was not matched by its consumer. Convert the value to a comparable numeric (e.g. .timestamp()) before floor/ceil, or reuse the datetime key handling.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The optimized path binds the datetime-ordered audit-log queryset (`order_by="-datetime"`, line 80) to `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, but that paginator's `get_item_key` (paginator.py:838-840) applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly to the order attribute. For this endpoint the attribute is `AuditLogEntry.datetime`, a datetime object, so `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError and the request 500s. The replaced `DateTimePaginator` existed precisely to convert datetime keys (e.g. `value.timestamp()`); OptimizedCursorPaginator only handles numeric keys. Either keep DateTimePaginator for datetime orderings or make OptimizedCursorPaginator datetime-aware.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new negative-offset branch assumes Django handles negative slicing ("properly handles negative slicing automatically"), but Django's QuerySet raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` whenever start/stop is negative. Since `Cursor` permits negative offsets (cursors.py parses `int(bits[1])` as-is and the new comment documents negative offsets as supported), a client can send e.g. `cursor=<v>:-5:0` with `enable_advanced_features=True` and hit `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `start_offset < 0`, producing a 500. Reject negative offsets (or clamp them) instead of slicing with them.

suggestions.suggestionContent: `_is_error_focused_query` decides whether to apply `upsampled_count()` by doing a naive substring search for `event.type:error` in the raw request query. A query that excludes errors (e.g. `!event.type:error`) or the discover-split query `({query}) AND event.type:transaction` still contains the literal `event.type:error`, so the transform is applied to a non-error / transactions query, summing `sample_weight` where it should be a plain `count()` and producing wrong bucket values. It also ignores the actual `query` passed to `_get_event_stats`, so the decision can differ from the query that is really executed. Match on a parsed/negation-aware condition (or pass the resolved query string) instead of a raw substring test.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The upsampling decision uses the closure variable `dataset` while the transformed `final_columns` are executed against `scoped_dataset`. In the dashboard-split path `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (e.g. `_get_event_stats(discover, ...)` at lines 351, 365, 406, 423) than the request's `dataset`, so the `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` branch can be evaluated against the wrong dataset and apply/skip `sum(sample_weight)` for a dataset that was never queried. Base the decision on the dataset actually being queried (`scoped_dataset`) so the transform matches the target of the query.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `upsampled_count` wraps the sum in `toInt64`, which truncates toward zero: `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` of e.g. 1.5 or 3.33 yields 1 or 3 instead of the nearest integer, systematically under-counting the upsampled estimate (worst when weights are just below an integer). Use a rounding aggregation (e.g. `toInt64(round(sum(...)))`) so the reconstructed count reflects the intended estimate rather than a floored value.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() shuts down the FixedQueuePool, but that pool is a singleton owned by the factory (created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and never recreated). Arroyo calls strategy.close() then join() on every assignment revocation/rebalance, and the factory's create_with_partitions is called again for the next assignment; the new strategy then reuses the already-shut-down queue_pool. Because q.shutdown(immediate=False) makes subsequent put() raise queue.ShutDown, submit()'s except branch (lines 317-325) swallows it and marks the offset complete, so after any rebalance every message is committed as processed without ever being handled — silent data loss. Fix: either let the factory own the pool lifecycle (don't shut it down from the strategy's close) and create a fresh pool per create_with_partitions, or reset/recreate factory.queue_pool when the strategy is closed.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: Each worker queue is created unbounded (queue.Queue() with no maxsize) although the class docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' and the strategy claims to guarantee backpressure. With no bound and no MessageRejected raised from submit(), a slow group continues to accumulate items in its queue while the consumer keeps polling, so memory grows without limit under a sustained backlog — the opposite of the intended protection. Fix: give the queues a maxsize and raise/return MessageRejected (or otherwise propagate backpressure to the caller) when a queue is full.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but the queues this strategy drives are unbounded: `FixedQueuePool` creates each one as `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize (line 185), and `submit()` puts items unconditionally. Nothing ever blocks, so no backpressure exists. Either bound the queues (pass a `maxsize` and handle `queue.Full` / block in `submit`) or correct the docstring so it does not advertise a guarantee the code does not provide.

suggestions.suggestionContent: The `WorkItem` docstring says it "includes the original message for offset tracking", but the `message` field is never used for offset tracking — `OffsetTracker` and the commit loop only ever read `partition`/`offset`, and `submit()` even re-derives the offset from `message.value` rather than from the stored `message`. Update the docstring to describe what the field is actually for (or remove the unused field) so it does not misdescribe the dataclass contract.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The commit assertion contradicts the test's own docstring and cannot fail for the reason it claims. The docstring says "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", but the body asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` — i.e. it passes only when nothing is committed. In queue_consumer.py ordered worker's `finally` calls `complete_offset` even after result_processor raises (lines 148-149), so offset 100 should be committable and offset 101 should advance the commit; if the whole commit path were removed (commits blocked entirely) the test would still pass. Assert the positive behaviour instead: e.g. that the failing message's offset was still completed so commits progressed (expect `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`, matching the follow-on offset of the successfully processed message).

The body only asserts all 6 items ran and that three distinct group numbers were seen — a single worker draining one queue, or a fully serial FixedQueuePool, would satisfy both assertions. Either measure actual overlap (e.g. have result_processor block on a barrier/event until all three groups have entered, and fail on timeout) or drop the concurrency claim from the name/docstring.

suggestions.suggestionContent: The worker marks the offset complete in the `finally` block even when `result_processor(...)` raises, so a message whose handling failed is reported as committable and its offset is committed (it will never be retried). This contradicts the strategy's own guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and the new test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, which asserts the partition is not committed after a failure. Only call `complete_offset` on the success path (or track failed offsets separately) so failures are not silently skipped.

The declared purpose does not match any actual use, so the field (and the extra reference to each Kafka message it keeps alive) is dead; either use it for offset tracking or remove it.

suggestions.suggestionContent: The worker marks the offset complete in `finally` even when `result_processor` raised an exception, so a failed item's offset is reported as committable and gets committed by the commit loop. This contradicts the strategy's documented guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and the contract asserted in test_results_consumer.py (test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, which expects the failed partition NOT to be committed): the failed message is committed past and never retried. Track success separately and only call `complete_offset` when processing succeeded (or make the failure explicit so the offset is withheld/retried).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The failed item's offset is completed unconditionally in the `finally` block, so `complete_offset` runs even when `result_processor` raised. This breaks the class's documented guarantee ('Only commits offsets after successful processing', line 254): the commit loop then advances past a message that was never successfully processed, silently dropping it (and, per the PR's own test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, a commit is produced where none is expected). Only call `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` on the success path (i.e. after `result_processor` returns normally), or explicitly decide and document the at-most-once semantics; do not complete on the exception path.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: ZUNIONSTORE uses AGGREGATE SUM by default, so when the same span payload is present in both `set_key` and the merged `span_key`/`parent_key` (duplicate delivery is anticipated by this buffer's own comments), its score is added instead of being kept equal to `end_timestamp_precise`. Because eviction at line 63 (`zpopmin` by score) compares scores across all members of `set_key`, a summed score makes the duplicated span appear far newer than its real end timestamp and biases eviction away from legitimately-old spans, breaking the stated 'evict oldest end timestamps' contract. Use ZUNIONSTORE ... AGGREGATE MIN (or MAX) so a duplicate keeps a single end timestamp score rather than doubling it.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: This hunk removes the only load-time span-count cap (`self.max_segment_spans`): previously a segment exceeding 1001 spans was logged, deleted from `payloads`/`cursors`, and skipped, but now every scanned span is unconditionally appended via `payloads[key].extend(...)`. The new bound relies entirely on insert-time eviction in the Lua script; if that eviction fails to bound a key (e.g. duplicated/scored members or the concurrent-writer case the code itself warns about at lines 457-461), this method will now materialize an unbounded number of spans into memory and emit them, whereas before it was safely skipped. Re-introduce a span-count guard (or verify the invite-time eviction strictly caps cardinality) to keep memory bounded.

suggestions.suggestionContent: `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` indexes the field directly (unlike the adjacent `parent_span_id`, which uses `.get`). This consumer did not read `end_timestamp_precise` before this PR, so any ingest payload that omits the field (older/replayed producers, partial schema) previously processed fine but now raises KeyError and aborts the entire batch. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise")` with a fallback (e.g. a span timestamp or 0.0) or explicitly validate/skip payloads missing the field.
